text: Richard Dawkins coined 'meme' in The Selfish Gene (1976), clipping the Greek mimeme, 'imitated thing', to sound like 'gene'. His examples were tunes, catchphrases, fashions and ways of building arches.

Mike Godwin launched Godwin's law on Usenet in 1990 as a deliberate experiment in memetics: 'As an online discussion grows longer, the probability of a comparison involving Nazis or Hitler approaches one.'
A 2016 model by physicist David Grimes estimated how quickly secrets leak. By his numbers, keeping the chance of exposure under 5% for just five years limits a conspiracy to about 2,500 people.

In a 2012 study, people who believed Princess Diana was murdered were more likely, not less, to believe she faked her own death. The authors concluded that distrust of the official story drives such beliefs.

Some conspiracies are real and documented. In 1962 the US Joint Chiefs of Staff proposed Operation Northwoods, staged attacks to be blamed on Cuba; President Kennedy rejected it, and the plan was made public in 1997.

Nick Bostrom's 2003 simulation argument does not say we are simulated. It says one of three holds: civilizations almost never mature, mature ones almost never run ancestor simulations, or we are almost surely in one.

Some 2,300 years ago the Chinese philosopher Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly. On waking, he wrote, he could not tell whether he was Zhuangzi who had dreamed of a butterfly or a butterfly now dreaming it was Zhuangzi.

Papyrus 115, one of the oldest manuscripts of Revelation, gives the beast's number as 616, not 666. Most scholars read both as Hebrew-letter sums for the emperor Nero, whose name had two common spellings.
A graffito at Pompeii reads, in Greek, 'I love her whose number is 545.' It relies on isopsephy, in which letters double as numerals, to hide the beloved's name in plain sight.

Since at least 1982 a Russian shortwave station on 4625 kHz, 'the Buzzer', has broadcast a monotonous buzz around the clock, now and then interrupted by a voice reading code words. No one has officially explained it.

Numbers stations are not just folklore. At the trial of Cuba's 'Wasp Network' spies, US prosecutors showed that the agents decoded orders from the shortwave station Atención, which read out strings of numbers.

In 373 BC an earthquake and tsunami swallowed the Greek city of Helike in one night. Its remains were found in 2001 beneath an ancient lagoon, and some scholars think its fate helped inspire Plato's Atlantis.

El Dorado was first a man, not a city: 'the gilded one', a ruler said to coat himself in gold dust and wash it off in a sacred lake. A gold Muisca raft found in Colombia in 1969 is often linked to that ritual.

On 4 January 2012 an anonymous post on 4chan launched Cicada 3301, a chain of cryptographic puzzles. Rounds followed in 2013 and 2014; the last is still unsolved, and the organizers have never been identified.
Radiocarbon tests in 2009 dated the vellum of the Voynich manuscript to 1404–1438. Its roughly 240 pages of unknown script and mostly unidentified plants have never been convincingly deciphered.

Easter Island's rongorongo script survives on only about two dozen wooden objects, none of them still on the island. Nobody can read it, and scholars still debate whether it is full writing or a memory aid.

Linear A can be sounded out, because its offspring Linear B was deciphered in 1952 and shares many signs. The words that emerge belong to an unknown Minoan language, so the texts still cannot be read.

The Antikythera mechanism, a geared bronze calculator from a Greek shipwreck of about 70–60 BC, predicted eclipses and tracked the Moon. Nothing comparable is known until the astronomical clocks of the 14th century.

The 'Baghdad battery', a clay jar holding a copper cylinder and an iron rod, was proposed as an ancient electric cell in 1938. Most archaeologists reject this and favor a ritual use, perhaps holding written spells.

From the late 1970s to 1995, US agencies funded 'remote viewing' in a program later called Stargate. A 1995 CIA-commissioned review found that no remote-viewing report had ever produced actionable intelligence.
When John White returned to Roanoke in 1590, the colonists were gone. He found 'CROATOAN' carved on a post but no cross, the sign they had agreed would mean distress, and their fate remains unknown.

The Mary Celeste was found adrift and deserted in 1872 with her cargo intact. Much of the legend, including the misspelling 'Marie Celeste', comes from an 1884 short story by a young Arthur Conan Doyle.

In December 1900 all three keepers of the Flannan Isles lighthouse in Scotland vanished. The eerie logbook entries often quoted about the case are fiction; the investigator concluded a huge wave swept them away.

The Bermuda Triangle has no unusual rate of losses. Lloyd's of London does not charge more to cross it, and Larry Kusche's 1975 study found many 'mysteries' involved storms, wrong locations or ships that came home.
Psychiatrist Robert Jay Lifton's 1961 study of thought reform described 'loading the language': high-control groups compress complex questions into 'thought-terminating clichés' that end discussion.

In Eileen Barker's study The Making of a Moonie (1984), most people who attended Unification Church workshops never joined, and many who did soon left, which undercut claims that recruits were simply brainwashed.
Renaissance scholars revered the Corpus Hermeticum as Egyptian wisdom older than Moses. In 1614 Isaac Casaubon showed from its Greek vocabulary that it was written in the early Christian era.
Tarot cards were invented in 15th-century Italy for a trick-taking card game. The idea that they encode ancient Egyptian wisdom began in 1781 with the French scholar Antoine Court de Gébelin.
Philosopher Nick Land coined 'hyperstition' in 1995 for an idea that makes itself real by circulating: a fiction that, once believed and acted on, helps bring about its own truth.

Slender Man has a birthday: 10 June 2009, when Eric Knudsen posted doctored photos to a Something Awful forum contest for paranormal images. Within a few years the character was being retold as folklore.
